data.title: Driver dies after Tesla collides with 2 cars on Hong Kong expressway
data.description:
A driver has died after a Tesla collided with a seven-seater on Hong Kong’s Island Eastern Corridor.
Police received a call at 10.37am on Saturday alerting them to a crash involving two private cars driving west along the corridor.
The force said the driver of one private vehicle was sent to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai while unconscious. The driver was later certified dead at 12.08pm.
It was not immediately clear which of the drivers died. The force said the incident remained under investigation.
Dashcam video of the incident circulating online showed a black Tesla drifting across lanes before colliding with a white seven-seater and another white vehicle, which drove away without stopping.
Images of the incident showed the airbags deployed in the Tesla while the right side of the white seven-seater was dented.
The Transport Department said that due to the accident, some Central-bound lanes of the Island East Corridor near North Point Ferry Pier were closed to traffic at one stage.

data.title: 3 arrested over allegedly seditious memorial outside Prince Edward MTR station
data.description:
Hong Kong national security police have arrested three people on suspicion of acting with seditious intent over a gathering outside Prince Edward MTR station to mark the 2019 protest flashpoint there.
A police force spokesman said on Saturday that two men and a woman were arrested on Thursday for allegedly shouting seditious slogans and holding white flowers outside the station on August 31.
“The people concerned were suspected of spreading false information and attacking the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government with lies,” the spokesman said.
He added that their acts were also suspected of smearing the police force with the intention of inciting hatred against the city government and its law enforcement agencies.

Prince Edward MTR station became a flashpoint during Hong Kong’s 2019 anti-government protests, when a controversial police operation on August 31 that year saw riot officers pursuing protesters into train carriages and beating people with batons and pepper spray.
That evening later gave rise to unsubstantiated claims of deaths, which police and government officials have repeatedly denied and denounced.
Memorial gatherings outside the busy MTR station subsequently became a near-monthly occurrence. At least 14 people were arrested in the Prince Edward neighbourhood during a 2020 memorial gathering.
The force spokesman denied allegations that an “incident” had taken place inside the station on August 31, 2019.
“It is a lie manipulated by people with ulterior motives to spread lies, attack the Hong Kong government and smear the police force, attempting to achieve their political objectives by endangering public peace,” the spokesman said.
The two men and one woman were arrested under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance for “doing an act with seditious intention”. The maximum punishment for the charge is seven years’ imprisonment.
Police also seized exhibits from the three arrestees’ residences, without disclosing what they were. Two remained in police custody as of Saturday afternoon with one bailed out from Hung Hom police station at 3pm.

data.title: Middle East war drives 35% rise in Hongkongers’ overseas help requests
data.description:
Hongkongers’ requests for help from overseas jumped 35 per cent in the first eight months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, the city’s immigration chief has revealed, attributing the rise to the war in the Middle East.
Director of Immigration Benson Kwok Joon-fung told reporters on Saturday that his department had received around 3,160 requests for assistance from Hong Kong residents overseas between January and August this year.
“The rise mainly came from the military conflict in the Middle East earlier this year. Of the rest, half involved lost identity documents,” Kwok said.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February. The conflict upended global air traffic as Middle Eastern flight hubs were deemed unsafe, disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and triggered a global fuel crisis.
Tensions at the strategic strait escalated again recently, prompting Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways to further cancel flights to Dubai and Riyadh up to and including November 30.
The immigration chief urged residents to keep a close eye on their passports and other personal identity documents when travelling overseas, as a lost document could hinder a person from leaving some countries.
“It also takes time to reissue the passport. Even though Chinese consulates and the Immigration Department will endeavour to help residents, it still takes some time,” Kwok said.

He also shed light on the soon-to-commission Huanggang Port checkpoint, the city’s second round-the-clock crossing after the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge control point.
He assured audiences that immigration systems had worked well during large-scale drills at the port over the past weeks.
The revamped Huanggang Port will be the first to use a “joint inspection” clearance model, where passengers need only present one identity document to cross the border, departing from traditional clearance methods that require travellers to clear two separate counters.
While the immigration chief said the opening date for the revamped crossing had yet to be decided, he added that city authorities and their Shenzhen counterparts had continued to make minor adjustments to various systems at the site.
Kwok said he expected the number of passengers using the revamped crossing to exceed 100,000 per day when it opened.
The department has also been trialling a new “seamless” e-channel clearance lane at the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge crossing since June, with an estimated 50,000 regular travellers of the land crossing allowed to join.
Kwok revealed on Saturday that 13,000 passengers had registered for the trial, with the two “seamless” lanes racking up around 80,000 uses so far.

data.title: In Focus|Will geopolitics put a potential Musk merger between a rocket and a hard place?
data.description:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.
The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.
In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.
But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces.
While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon.
That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies.
Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers.
“Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
“But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.”
The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together.
Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another
Seth Goldstein, Morningstar
Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics.
While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation.
“Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein.
The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said.
Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders.
The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”.
“This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter.
Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject.


Can Tesla do without China?
At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025.
Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale.
Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers.
Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line.
Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.
Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced. It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain.
China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS.




“Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said.
“That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.”
Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added.
Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account.
Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May.
Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors.
And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies.
The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised
Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney
Between Washington and Beijing
Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor.
Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May.
Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus.
The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June.
But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”.
Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations.
How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang.
“The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.”
She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.”


Tesla lays the first bricks
Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China.
It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry.
Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said.
CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market.
Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience.
“A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.
Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said.
SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology.




Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments.
However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake.
While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said.
Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’
However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”.
“So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.”
Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call.
A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator.
Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US.


“There is an overlap in key‑component supply chains between Optimus and Tesla EVs, and Tesla leverages existing Chinese partners to co-develop and produce joint modules, dexterous hands and other key parts,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at Counterpoint Research.
Tier-one suppliers including Tuopu Group, Zhejiang Sanhua, Xusheng Group and Glory Mica are veterans in Tesla’s EV value chain with years of proven partnerships, according to Qi. “They fully back Optimus V3’s mass production plan,” he said.
Amid geopolitical uncertainties, these Chinese partners would willingly relocate or expand their capacity beyond China to mitigate the impacts of tariffs, as they anticipate strong sales prospects from Optimus, Qi added.
These delicate and complex adjustments could move fast. Ark Investment Management’s chief futurist Brett Winton said he expected a SpaceX and Tesla combination to be announced before the end of 2026.
Tesla’s China operations could pose a “smallish wrinkle” in a potential merger with SpaceX, a major US defence contractor, but it was not necessarily “a stumbling block”, Winton said in a video podcast posted on X on August 11.
“The fact that Tesla owns its own factory there is really an anomaly … and an underestimated testament to Elon Musk’s ability to navigate political choppiness in different ways,” Winton said.
Rather than addressing the questions raised by the podcast directly, Musk responded on X with an endorsement that has become commonplace for the CEO.
“China is awesome. I strongly encourage people to visit.”

data.title: China’s AI ‘little giant’ Yunxi Technology files for Hong Kong IPO: sources
data.description:
Yunxi Technology, officially one of China’s “little giants”, has submitted a confidential initial public offering application to Hong Kong’s stock exchange, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Guangzhou-based start-up was valued at 10 billion yuan (US$1.27 billion) in its latest private funding round and was working with Bocom International on the deal, aiming to raise “several hundred million [US] dollars”, said the people, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue.
While the listing is targeted to take place by the end of this year, the timing and size remain subject to change, the people said. High-profile backers include Chinese billionaire Jack Ma’s Yunfeng Capital and investment firm HSG Capital.
Yunxi did not immediately respond to South China Morning Post’s request for comment.
Founded in 2016, Yunxi provides end-to-end digital growth products and tools to help major clients across the consumer goods, retail, real estate and automotive sectors integrate artificial intelligence into their operations.
The company is one of China’s nationally recognised “little giants”, a label awarded by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology to specialised, innovative small- and medium-sized enterprises that focus on niche markets, master core technologies and hold high market shares.
By November 2025, China had nurtured over 17,600 such firms, with plans to expand that total to 22,000 by 2030, according to a recent ministry notice.
According to a source familiar with the transaction, Yunxi had applied to list under Chapter 18C of the Hong Kong stock exchange rules – a specialised framework designed for high-growth firms in advanced technology sectors.
Official data from the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing showed that by the end of March, 14 companies had gone public under this specific chapter, raising a combined HK$28.4 billion (US$3.62 billion), with additional applications under review.

data.title: Visitors urge Hong Kong to ease restrictions as Sai Kung trail registration begins
data.description:
Hundreds of Hong Kong residents and visitors braved the heat on Saturday morning to visit a popular Sai Kung trail overlooking hexagonal rock columns, as a trial reservation system requiring real-name registration came into force, with some calling for the restrictions to be eased.
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department announced the arrangement last month, capping visitor numbers at 2,000 per designated day between 9am and 5pm for the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail.
The measure is Hong Kong’s first countryside real-name reservation system of its kind.
Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department director Mickey Lai Kin-ming said that, as of 10.10am, about 140 visitors had arrived at Po Pin Chau — a figure similar to that on previous weekends.
He added that the verification process had gone smoothly and that about 50 unused slots had been released to walk-in visitors.
Among the first visitors to Po Pin Chau under the registration system was Doreen Sun, a tourist from Beijing who had not previously visited the trail.
The education professional, in her thirties, said she had planned her four-day trip to Hong Kong specifically to hike and visited Po Pin Chau with a friend after seeing recommendations on the mainland social media platform RedNote.
“There is a need for such a registration system,” she said. “The presence of many staff here also guarantees safety.”

The department previously said the system was put in place to protect the narrow trail from excessive wear and tear, prevent overcrowding and improve the visitor experience, adding that the quota would be further reviewed.
No fees will be charged for bookings or penalties for failing to turn up – at least for now.
The roughly 1km-long (1094-yard) trail is within the Unesco Global Geopark at Sai Kung East Country Park and passes giant hexagonal volcanic rock columns dramatically jutting out from the sea, providing a viewing platform overlooking them.
Hongkonger Moon Kok booked the 11am slot to take her mother, with whom she lives, and her aunt, who was visiting from Guangzhou, to Po Pin Chau for the first time.
“The booking system itself was not difficult, but it would be better if we could amend the booking before our visits, such as adding an extra person,” said the researcher, who is in her twenties.


She added that some family members had been unable to join them as a result.
Kok said the number of visitors on the trail was comfortable at its current level, but warned that any more would feel excessive and could create safety concerns, given the narrow and steep steps.
Her mother also suggested that authorities should indicate the difficulty of the hike so prospective visitors could assess whether it was suitable for them
The reservation system applies to Saturdays and Sundays from September 5 to 20, the three-day weekend over the Mid-Autumn Festival starting on September 25, and October 1 to 7 – mainland China’s National Day “golden week” holiday.
Authorities have set a quota of 500 visitors for each of the four two-hour time slots available on those days.

Visitors need to book through Klook on a first-come, first-served basis, with slots opening as early as 11am on August 24. Those wishing to visit before 9am or after 5pm can enter the area without a reservation.
During previous golden week holiday periods, popular beaches were littered with rubbish, with reports of visitors at environmentally sensitive areas trampling on coral reefs while snorkelling and catching marine creatures.
The reports sparked controversy, prompting authorities to cordon off certain areas and experts to call for a comprehensive, top-down ecotourism policy led by a single designated authority to safeguard the environment.

data.title: Hong Kong’s billionaires, Treasury yields hit 4.78%: the numbers moving markets
data.description:
China has been expanding its outbound-investment channels, with a new quota granted and greater overseas allocation by the nation’s pension fund. However, the financial world beyond the mainland is seeing volatility as US bond yields hit 20-month highs.
Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week.
US$6.84 billion in new quotas for mutual funds
China’s foreign-exchange regulator approved US$6.84 billion in new, qualified domestic institutional investor (QDII) quotas for mutual funds, insurers and banks’ wealth-management units by the end of August, according to data from the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, expanding their capacity to invest in overseas assets.
Eighteen money managers, including China Asset Management and GF Fund Management, received US$100 million each, while more than 20 Chinese banks’ wealth-management units received quotas for the first time.
Hong Kong has 106 billionaires, second only to New York
Hong Kong remained the world’s second-largest billionaire hub with 106 billionaires, trailing only New York, which had 164, according to wealth data provider Altrata.
Beijing and Shenzhen also ranked among the world’s 15 cities with the most billionaires, helped by wealth creation from the AI boom.
US 10-year Treasury yield hits 20-month high
The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.78 per cent on Tuesday, its highest level in 20 months, as investors sold government debt amid concerns over the country’s fiscal outlook.
The move came as US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told G20 finance ministers that Washington was a leader in tackling sovereign debt problems in emerging markets, even as rising borrowing costs in the US highlighted the challenges facing the country. Benchmark yields in Japan and the UK have also climbed to multi-decade highs.
China’s national pension offshore assets hit record US$86 billion
China’s National Social Security Fund more than doubled its offshore investments in three years to a record 580.02 billion yuan (US$86 billion) at the end of 2025, as it sought higher returns through greater exposure to overseas markets.
Offshore assets accounted for 15.23 per cent of the fund’s total assets, the highest proportion on record, according to its annual report released on Tuesday.

data.title: Overhead display left dangling at airport’s Terminal 2, investigation under way
data.description:
An overhead electronic display was left dangling in the air at Hong Kong airport’s newly reopened Terminal 2, prompting authorities to pledge a detailed investigation.
A spokesman said the incident occurred at about 8.30am on Saturday, when a suspended screen “experienced a technical fault”, triggering its fall-arrest safety system.
“The Airport Authority takes the incident very seriously and will conduct a detailed investigation into the cause, with a view to further enhancing the stability of the system,” the spokesman said.
Terminal 2’s departure facilities reopened on May 27 as part of the airport’s HK$141.5 billion (US$18.1 billion) three-runway system upgrade.

Passengers using the terminal can check in, clear immigration and undergo security screening there before returning to Terminal 1 for departure.
A maintenance team promptly attended to the malfunctioning screen and cordoned off the area, the authority said.
Photos and videos of the incident circulated widely on social media, with users expressing outrage over a safety hazard emerging just months after the terminal’s reopening.
Footage posted on Threads shows the circular screens swaying, secured to the ceiling by two cables.
“Terminal 2’s design is great. Having spent a few hundred million Hong Kong dollars, the whole thing was about to collapse within a few months of opening,” one user said.

data.title: Hong Kong’s leader outlines 3 key new growth drivers ahead of first 5-year plan
data.description:
Hong Kong’s leader has identified financial services, innovation and technology, and education as three key new growth drivers ahead of the unveiling of the city’s inaugural five-year development blueprint and annual policy address.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Saturday that Hong Kong’s first five-year plan would outline broad strategies, set clear development directions and align with the nation’s 15th five-year plan, while the policy address would focus on specific measures.
He said the two documents were closely linked and mutually reinforcing.
“We will remain pragmatic, continue to unleash market vitality, and constantly cultivate new growth drivers for Hong Kong,” he said of the city’s five-year plan.
Lee highlighted four initiatives that he said had injected new momentum and created fresh opportunities: ensuring the effective operation of the central gold clearing system; developing a commodities trading ecosystem; attracting leading global enterprises to the Hetao innovation hub, the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park in the Lok Ma Chau Loop; and developing a university town in the Northern Metropolis.
Benjamin Hung Pi-cheng, chairman of the government think tank Financial Services Development Council, said the establishment of the Hong Kong Gold Exchange in January last year was a strategic and visionary move.

“There is only a handful of markets in the world that provide services of trading, refinery and storage of gold, and Hong Kong aims to be among these three-in-one markets,” he said. “The development is also timely along with intensifying geopolitics, as capital is flowing from the west to the east.”
Hung said gold was the starting point for the development of the commodities ecosystem, which would later be extended to other precious metals.
“This will ultimately enhance the city to have the pricing power and more say in the precious metals market,” he said.
Vincent Ma, CEO of the Hetao technology park, said the innovation hub had attracted more than 100 technology companies, providing a solid foundation for further development.
He said the completion of the innovation park’s main building, originally scheduled for a later date, had been brought forward to the end of this year, with its initial occupancy rate expected to reach 75 per cent.
Tim Lui Tim-leung, chairman of the government’s University Grants Committee, said the university town at the Northern Metropolis would cover more than 1,000 hectares (2,471 acres), including 300 hectares of campus space.

“The university town will be developed with five elements, education, technology, talents, industries and urban development,” he said. “We will transform Hong Kong’s academic research into the power of commercialisation.”
China’s 15th five-year plan, covering 2026 to 2030, requires Hong Kong to contribute to the nation’s development. It also supports the city’s efforts to become a high-end talent hub and to consolidate and enhance its status as an international financial, shipping and trading centre.
Lee said the government had received a strong response to an earlier public consultation on the city’s five-year plan, describing the feedback as “valuable and diversified” and as “providing an important reference and revelation”.
During the two-month consultation, which ended in late August, the government held more than 100 sessions to gather views, with Lee personally conducting about 30 of them.
It received more than 16,000 public submissions. About 80 per cent came from individuals and focused on livelihood issues, while the rest were submitted by organisations, including political parties, think tanks, academic groups and business chambers.
Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the annual policy address are due to be announced on September 16.

data.title: AI boom is hiding cracks in US markets, Nomura warns
data.description:
The artificial intelligence boom has signalled growing risks in the US economy and capital markets, with a setback in the technology rally potentially triggering a sharp correction in US assets and weakening the dollar, according to a Nomura report.
“The AI boom has masked a rising US risk premium,” Nomura analysts led by Rob Subbaraman said in a report on Thursday, warning that the concentration of global savings in US dollar assets had left investors increasingly exposed to a reversal in the AI-driven US equity rally.
The ratio of US net international investment position (NIIP) liabilities to the combined assets of all net creditor nations has risen to 80 per cent, according to the Japanese investment bank.
US NIIP liabilities reached US$21.9 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 71 per cent of gross domestic product, while the country’s portfolio liabilities have quadrupled to US$37.4 trillion in March 2026 from US$9.2 trillion before the global financial crisis, the bank’s data showed.
“We attempt to debunk the assumed robustness of ‘Tina’,” the bank said, referring to the belief that “there is no alternative” to US assets.
The growing exposure meant a sharp decline in US equities could have broader implications for global capital flows, particularly if foreign investors began to reduce their holdings of US assets, according to Nomura.
Despite the strong profit growth of US equities supported by the AI boom, the bank flagged high valuations, uncertain adoption, competition from cheaper Chinese large language models (LLMs) and constraints on computing power, memory and electricity.
A setback in AI could expose vulnerabilities masked by the equity rally and trigger a broader risk-off move, according to the bank.
Foreign investors’ large exposure to US portfolio assets, together with leverage and circular financing linked to the AI investment boom, could amplify the impact, it added.
Nomura estimated that US portfolio assets would need to fall by more than 30 per cent – comparable to a global financial crisis-scale repatriation – to fully offset the decline in US portfolio liabilities.

data.title: After 66 years, Kau Kee shop offers fish balls ‘every Hongkonger has eaten’
data.description:
Anita Lee Yan-kwan grew up around a traditional business that supplied fish balls to Hong Kong’s street food stalls and eateries. But for decades, Kau Kee Food Factory’s signature product was known only among industry operators until Lee, a second-generation owner, opened the company’s first retail store late last year.
Kau Kee has operated as a silent giant in the food industry for 66 years, supplying its fish balls to nearly 1,000 eateries and snack stalls across the city. But it finally opened its first bricks-and-mortar shop in Mong Kok last December.
“Before opening the retail shop, if you were to ask people about Kau Kee on the street, they would probably not know about it,” Lee said. “Yet it’s likely almost every Hongkonger has eaten our fish balls.”
The 30-year-old politics graduate and former civil servant made a career pivot during the Covid-19 pandemic and took charge of the family business even as mask mandates and social distancing rules crippled the street food scene.
It left Kau Kee, which was relying solely on manufacturing and wholesaling at the time, in a precarious position as orders from food stalls dropped drastically.
“Our business took a really big hit and was severely affected. Since everyone was wearing masks, they stopped eating fish balls on the street. With the economy being so poor, people were spending less money overall,” Lee said.
She launched the company’s first online store to sell the products directly to consumers in 2023.


Lee recalled how anxious she was about running a factory business at the outset – to say nothing of meeting her parents’ expectations.
“Our entire background and expertise was in factory manufacturing. I needed to figure out how to scale production and perfect standard operating procedures,” she said.
“Running a retail store requires a completely different skill set. It involves managing people, inventory and, most dauntingly, marketing and promotion – areas where a traditional brand has the least experience.
“It’s been a massive challenge because we are starting from scratch.”
To compete, Lee leaned into the brand’s greatest strength by cutting out third-party mark-ups and reselling fees and offering its products at a nostalgic “throwback price” of HK$10 (US$1.28) for 10 pieces – roughly half the current market average.
“Since we are a factory selling directly to our own shop, we have eliminated the middleman,” Lee explained.
“Removing that extra layer means we can give back to the customer. We want people to know that a lower price doesn’t mean inferior ingredients. It simply means better value because we are reaching the consumer directly.”
Unlike mass-produced supermarket versions designed for immediate consumption at home, Kau Kee’s recipe was specifically engineered for the street food environment, she said.
“Our fish balls contain more fish meat so they stay chewy and don’t become soggy or bloated, even after soaking in curry sauce for half an hour or longer at a busy food stall.”

Lee also revealed the secret ingredient to their shop’s signature “king of fish balls” – tuna.
“Adding tuna is special because it has a high fat content, giving the fish balls a rich, fragrant oiliness you can really taste,” she said.
Lee’s modernisation of the brand also includes “Instagrammable” touches, such as a 3D-printed oversized fish ball model, which has helped attract a new generation of customers and tourists, who now make up about 30 per cent of her customer base.
For Lee, the venture is about ensuring the pulse of the 66-year-old business continues to beat while planning her next storefront.
“I hope the first store is just a starting point,” she said. “I hope the many years of history will continue.”
Driven by a sense of cultural pride, Lee has experienced a mounting sense of frustration at seeing local icons overshadowed by an influx of foreign snack chains.
“Nowadays, there are more types of snacks from Korea and Taiwan. But for Hong Kong-style snacks like fish balls and siumai, it feels like only a few old shops are left and they are slowly declining,” she said.
“This is a vital part of Hong Kong’s history that has accompanied so many of us. There is no reason for shops from elsewhere to thrive here while we don’t”.

data.title: How some grey-market crypto ATMs in Hong Kong can turn users into fraud victims
data.description:
Inside a tiny self-service laundromat in Quarry Bay in the east of Hong Kong Island, next to a wall of washing machines, stands a waist-high cryptocurrency terminal with signs reading “Elon Musk recommends Dogecoin” and “Buy bitcoin in one minute”.
In order to obtain Dogecoin through the ATM, customers feed Hong Kong dollar notes into a slot and scan a QR code. The equivalent amount in cryptocurrency is then credited into their digital wallet.
Such machines have proliferated across the city in recent years as interest in cryptocurrencies has risen. Many are installed at 24-hour unstaffed shops such as laundromats and claw-machine arcades.
As of 2024, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) found about 200 virtual asset retailers in the city, which included such ATMs.
According to Coin ATM Radar, a global geographical tracker, there are currently 234 crypto ATMs in Hong Kong – concentrated in Mong Kok, Tsim Sha Tsui, Wan Chai and Quarry Bay – offering a dozen different types of cryptocurrencies.
However, these ATMs operate in a legal grey area, with the city still in the process of setting up a regulatory regime for over-the-counter cryptocurrency trading.
Potential tools in financial scams
Some lawmakers and industry insiders warned people of the potential investment risks associated with scams, weak consumer protection and money laundering that ATMs posed.
Legislator Johnny Ng Kit-chong said scams involving ATM cryptocurrency transfers were growing increasingly common across the world and often took two forms.
The first was through fraudulent machines that accepted cash but did not dispense any crypto, or vice versa. The second was through human actors, such as when fraudsters posed as officials or wooed targets romantically to get them to transfer cash or crypto through a fake ATM controlled by the scammers.
“Because blockchain-backed transactions are irreversible and ATMs lack robust verification, recovering these funds is nearly impossible,” Ng said.
Two operators, Coinhero and Coinunit, claim to be running Asia’s largest crypto network. A check on their websites found that Coinhero lists its transaction fees online and offers customer support via WhatsApp, email and an actual flagship store in Causeway Bay, while Coinunit’s only channel is a web contact form.

Another operator is Canada-based Localcoin. Its CEO, Tristan Fong, said the company had 30 ATMs in Hong Kong and operated consumer protection controls remotely.
“We have best-in-class, real-time on-and-off-chain transaction monitoring tools that can be deployed anywhere on earth,” he said.
Fong acknowledged the risks of money laundering and scams but noted that other financial services also faced such risks. His company monitored transactions and issued scam warnings to combat illicit activity.
Fong welcomed the city’s planned regulation and dialogue with lawmakers on rules for the sector.
“Clear rules in Hong Kong would protect consumers, raise standards across the industry, and benefit operators with the ability to implement strong and sophisticated controls,” he said.
“We look forward to reviewing the framework when it is published. We will comply fully with any new requirements.”
The South China Morning Post has reached out to Coinhero for comment.
Regulatory proposal in the works
In response to queries from the SCMP, the Financial Services and Treasury Bureau said it was finalising legislative proposals with the SFC to regulate virtual asset dealers, including crypto ATM operators, virtual asset custodians and advisory and management service providers.
“We are now finalising the legislative proposals, with a target of introducing the relevant bill into the Legislative Council later this year,” it said.
The bureau stressed that operators should also “comply with other applicable laws and regulations in Hong Kong”.
Andrew Fei, a partner at law firm King & Wood, said that even without a dedicated virtual asset dealer licensing regime, ATM operators remained bound by the city’s existing statutes, including criminal laws.
But a specific licence would impose more robust consumer protection, know-your-customer standards, financial resources, risk management and other requirements to help ensure that crypto ATMs were operated in a safe and compliant manner, he added.
Fei said shop owners who allowed crypto ATMs on their premises appeared to have straightforward commercial motives, such as drawing foot traffic, and their legal exposure hinged on what they “reasonably” knew about the operators’ legitimacy.
“For criminal liability to attach to shop owners that merely allow the ATMs to be placed in their premises, they would need to have at least some knowledge or suspicion that the ATM operator is doing something illegal,” Fei said.
“If they don’t know or suspect anything, then I don’t think the shop owner would be criminally liable.”

He suggested that regulators establish an orderly timeline to allow existing market participants to prepare for and obtain the new virtual asset dealing licence before the regime formally comes into effect, to avoid disruption of existing client-facing activities, especially those carried out by financial institutions.
Singapore bans crypto ATMs. Other jurisdictions such as Australia allow such services, despite the government’s warning in 2025 that such machines are “one of the highest risk money laundering channels”.
Future demand and legitimacy of crypto operators
Syed Musheer Ahmed, the founder of Advisory FinStep Asia, a fintech, crypto, and virtual asset advisory firm, said customers of cryptocurrency ATMs in Hong Kong could be small-amount crypto investors, or visitors from jurisdictions where crypto trading was forbidden.
“The broader crypto exchange activities globally have come down in the past six months,” Ahmed said, noting that the retail interest for local investors could have gone down.
As of Friday, one bitcoin traded at about US$80,630.
An SCMP reporter who observed the Quarry Bay laundromat for three hours on a weekday afternoon found that not a single person used the ATM.
Fong of LocalCoin said demand for cash-to-crypto transactions had cooled in Hong Kong, with both transaction volumes and average sizes declining. But he argued ATMs were still useful for consumers seeking quick access to digital assets.
“We’ve also seen ever-growing numbers of fake crypto exchange websites,” he said. “Concerns about these websites also drive first-time crypto buyers to our machines, because their physical presence in a trusted retail location creates a high level of comfort.”
Leon Liu, a researcher at the blockchain network Tron, said the location of the ATMs was not incidental, as laundromats and claw machine arcades were typically unstaffed and opened round the clock – a business model that minimised the cost of running ATMs.
But Jack Poon, professor of practice in fintech and entrepreneurial finance at Polytechnic University, warned that unstaffed machines could be platforms for money laundering, as users had no way of knowing whether the cryptocurrency they received came from a legitimate source or illegal activity.

He also pointed to the collapse of cryptocurrency platform JPEX, which allegedly committed the city’s biggest financial fraud involving HK$1.6 billion (US$204.1 million) and more than 2,700 victims in 2023, as a cautionary precedent for what happened when an operator had no accountable presence in the city.
“A lot of people put money in there without protection. When the operator pulled the plug, a lot of people suffered,” he said. “It was very difficult for Hong Kong law enforcement or regulators to help investors recover their money because the entity was not even in Hong Kong.”
According to police, 969 cryptocurrency-related cases were recorded in the first six months of this year, with losses totalling HK$2.68 billion. Those losses amounted to 77.9 per cent of the figure in all of 2025.
The number of cases declined by 11.1 per cent to 2,234 in 2025 from a year earlier, while the figure in 2024 was 2,513, a 26.4 per cent drop from 3,415 in 2023. Losses in 2025 totalled HK$3.44 billion, down by 1.7 per cent from 2024.
Police did not record the breakdown of cases related only to crypto ATMs.

data.title: 2 floors of Rumsey Street car park to close for 6 weeks for Interpol meeting use
data.description:
A public multi-storey car park in Hong Kong’s central business district will be partially closed for about six weeks from November as the city prepares to host a meeting of Interpol’s top governing body for the first time.
Hong Kong police plan to take over the seventh and eighth floors of the Rumsey Street car park in Sheung Wan to set up a traffic coordination command centre.
“The centre is planned to accommodate 240 electric cars to be used by participants of Interpol’s general assembly travelling to and from the airport, hotels and meeting venues,” the police force said in a paper to be tabled for discussion at a meeting of Central and Western District Council next Thursday.
“The seventh and eighth floors of the car park will be used as a traffic coordination command centre from November 1, 2026. After the general assembly concludes, it will reopen to the public on December 12.”
The car park was chosen because it was on Hong Kong Island and close to hotels and the meeting venue, “which is conducive to the coordination and dispatch of vehicles” for the conference, police said.
The 94th Interpol general assembly will be held from November 30 to December 3 at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai.
While Hong Kong is making its debut as host, it marks China’s third time, with Beijing having hosted in 1995 and 2017.

The general assembly is Interpol’s highest governing body, with member countries gathering to discuss international policing issues and foster collaboration.
Interpol has 196 member countries. Hong Kong participates as part of China’s Interpol national delegation, operating locally as a sub-bureau under Beijing’s National Central Bureau.
City officials have said that hosting the event in Hong Kong serves to demonstrate the professional image of the city, while Hong Kong police are committed to enhancing collaboration within the global law enforcement community.
Police said they would monitor traffic conditions and take measures to ensure smooth traffic flow around the car park while the two floors were closed.
The Rumsey Street facility is one of 10 government-run multi-storey car parks. It has nearly 1,000 parking spaces for cars, vans, and motorcycles. The top floors of the building are occupied by government offices while the lower levels are used as a public car park.

data.title: Chinese carmaker Chery to begin testing solid-state EV batteries next yearChairman says it plans to invest US$1.49 billion in the new battery technology over the next two years.
data.description:
Chery Automobile, China’s largest car exporter by deliveries, will begin testing its solid-state batteries next year, aiming to spearhead commercialisation of a technology likely to further spur the electrification of the global automotive industry.
Yin Tongyue, the chairman of the state-owned carmaker, which is based in central China’s Anhui province, said on Thursday that it would invest 10 billion yuan (US$1.49 billion) in the new battery technology over the next two years, with 1,200 engineers to be deployed in the hunt for innovative breakthroughs.
“Multiple [battery] technology plans are being laid out,” he told the World Power Battery Conference in Yibin, Sichuan province, the National Business Daily reported. “We will not install them in our vehicles unless they prove to be absolutely safe.”
He said the solid-state batteries to be tested next year would have an energy density of 400 watt-hours per kilogram, double that of the batteries used in existing electric vehicles (EVs).
Solid-state batteries, which use a solid electrolyte to conduct ions between electrodes, are widely seen as a superior alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on liquid or ­gel-based materials. Analysts said the technology promised higher energy density, improved safety and longer driving range.
Even if the new tech gets mature, battery makers have to bring down the costs to make it affordable to consumers
Eric Han, Suolei
But no solid-state batteries have been installed in mass-produced EVs.
And just a handful of cars – such as some premium models from Shanghai-based Nio – use semi-solid-state batteries, where liquid is added to solid electrolytes to improve performance.
Compared with liquid-based batteries, solid-state variants are less prone to overheating or catching fire in the event of overcharging or collisions.
Yin did not reveal when Chery cars equipped with solid-state batteries could hit the market.
In June, Robin Zeng Yuqun, chairman of Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL), the world’s largest EV battery producer, told a forum that mass production of solid-state batteries would not happen until 2030.
On a scale of one to nine, the technology had only reached level four to date, he said.
Eric Han, a senior ­manager at Shanghai consultancy Suolei, said Yin and Zeng’s contrasting views might “attract more attention from the public as more drivers in China are now opting for electric cars”.
“Even if the new tech gets mature, battery makers have to bring down the costs to make it affordable to consumers,” he said.

data.title: Robot guide dog debuts in China amid severe lack of the furry kind
data.description:
A Chinese defence industry research facility has unveiled what it calls the world’s first wheeled and legged robot guide dog for visually impaired people, in an example of the sector’s push into a growing range of civilian applications.
Hangzhou-based Zhiyuan Research Institute, affiliated with China North Industries Group, the country’s largest defence contractor, launched the robot, dubbed Xiaoyuan, on Friday at the China Care and Rehabilitation Expo in Beijing.
Equipped with wheels for smooth movement on flat ground and four legs for climbing stairs, the robot was designed to help visually impaired people navigate independently, according to the institute.
The wheeled design allowed the robot to move quietly, an important feature for those who rely on their hearing to perceive their surroundings, the institute said. Meanwhile, it could also identify overhead obstacles such as low-hanging branches, which could be difficult to detect with traditional mobility aids such as canes.
The robot offered centimetre-level outdoor positioning accuracy, with an error margin of less than 30 centimetres, while its obstacle-avoidance success rate was at least 99 per cent indoors and 96 per cent outdoors, according to the institute.
Xiaoyuan is connected to services including disability federation systems, an accessibility map and a remote assistance portal for volunteers, allowing users to seek help remotely when needed.
China has more than 17 million people with visual impairments, according to a report by state-run Xinhua News in May, citing the China Association of Persons with Visual Disabilities (CAPVD).
By comparison, the country has only around 400 guide dogs in service, according to CAPVD, which added that a guide dog costs around 200,000 yuan (US$29,776) and takes about a year to train.


The institute said it had reached strategic cooperation agreements with disability groups in the eastern province of Zhejiang, its capital Hangzhou and Inner Mongolia, and had begun pilot deployments and trials at locations including Hangzhou’s metro system and shopping centres.
Other developers are also working on expanding the application of robotics and AI in China.
For example, Beijing-based AI Robotics and Hangzhou-based RoboCT have developed exoskeleton robots used at hospitals and rehabilitation centres to help patients regain mobility.

data.title: IVF clinic’s embryo specimen mix-up linked to ‘intentional unlawful conduct’
data.description:
A mix-up of embryo biopsy specimens may have been caused by “intentional unlawful conduct” at a private fertility clinic, which breached the code of practice for reproductive technology by lacking sufficient protective measures, a Hong Kong regulator has found.
The Council on Human Reproductive Technology said on Friday that, following an investigation into the incident, it had ordered service provider Heal Fertility to comply with the Human Reproductive Technology Ordinance and the code to prevent any recurrence of similar incidents.
“The council confirmed that no embryos were mixed up or wrongly implanted into the human body in the incident,” it said.
The council also put the clinic’s licence under review.
It concluded that “intentional unlawful conduct by an individual” was the main cause of the embryo biopsy specimen mix-up at Heal Fertility’s clinic in Central.
The council said it would continue to provide professional support to police in an ongoing criminal investigation into the case.
The incident came to light earlier this year when a genetic testing laboratory at the Chinese University of Hong Kong found that embryo biopsy specimens sent by Heal Fertility did not belong to the intended patients.
Only one of seven specimens from the first woman was hers, while neither of two specimens attributed to the second woman was correct.
The clinic, which opened in 2023 as part of the New Frontier Group co-founded by former financial secretary Antony Leung Kam-chung, was notified of the mismatches on May 26 and June 4.
The council subsequently suspended most operations at the clinic.
Council chairman Professor Raymond Liang Hin-suen said the Department of Health had filed a police report.

A Malaysian employee responsible for extracting the specimens was interviewed by police in late July but left Hong Kong the following day and resigned.
She is now wanted in connection with a fraud investigation handled by the organised crime and triad bureau.
Heal Fertility apologised to affected clients and submitted an internal investigation report to health authorities on July 29.
The council also noted that Heal Fertility, after identifying the mix-up, did not report the incident to the department within the required time frame.
It reminded the clinic that all licensed day procedure centres must strictly comply with licence conditions set by the Council, the Department of Health and relevant codes.
While Heal Fertility has since implemented improvement measures regarding the handling and storage arrangements of embryos and embryo biopsy specimens, the council’s assessment of the clinic’s response remained guarded.
“There is still room for further enhancement in Heal Fertility’s overall performance and operational arrangements,” it said.
The council said it had drawn up improvement requirements, would issue a formal letter on Friday and reinspect the premises before making a licensing decision.
Until then, Heal Fertility may only provide three services related to the storage of gametes or embryos.
Separately, the council has resolved to review the code of practice, targeting completion next year.
Key areas include strengthening the incident reporting mechanism and optimising security and handling procedures for biological samples.

data.title: Dairy Queen to return to Hong Kong with 4 stores. Is it scooping up cheap rents?
data.description:
American ice cream chain Dairy Queen will open four Hong Kong outlets in the fourth quarter of this year, as part of an ambitious expansion plan amid a wave of food and retail shop closures across the city.
Dairy Queen, an 85-year-old brand, said on Friday that it would launch its flagship store at One Causeway Bay shopping centre on Hong Kong Island in November, followed by three other outlets in Kowloon, the New Territories and the outlying islands before the end of the year.
“Following Causeway Bay, the Kwun Tong store in Kowloon is already under hoarding,” the company said. “A total of four stores are set to open this quarter, strategically covering Hong Kong Island, Kowloon, the New Territories and the outlying islands.”
The Kwun Tong store is located in The Angle shopping centre. The coming stores mark the brand’s return to Hong Kong after a short-lived opening in Causeway Bay in 1979.
The company said it had a fresh store concept tailored for Hong Kong, featuring five product lines, including milkshakes, parfaits and uniquely designed ice cream cakes.
It said the city’s products would include its signature soft-serve dessert, which it described as “thick enough to hold when the cup is turned upside down” and made with an exclusive full-fat dairy mix and an air overrun of about 40 per cent to maintain texture.
Edwin Lee Kan-hing, founder and chief executive of Bridgeway Prime Shop Fund Management, said Dairy Queen’s entry into the market comes after a sharp fall in retail rents and shop values, creating lower entry costs for foreign brands even as legacy merchants using older business models continue to shut down.
Traditional dim sum and Chinese restaurants have been closing across the city, with the Star Seafood Restaurant Group closing numerous branches in 2025 and this year, and the 35-year-old Metropol Restaurant in Admiralty shutting in September last year.
“Out with the old and in with the new,” Lee said, pointing out that commercial rents in core districts had dropped by 60 to 70 per cent from peak levels in 2013 and 2014.

With lower rents and strong tourist spending power, more foreign brands would enter Hong Kong, he said.
“It would not be surprising if two or three out of every 10 new outlets eventually close,” Lee said.
He also characterised Dairy Queen’s decision to open four branches across four different parts of the city as a marketing tactic intended to gain rapid visibility.
“The weather is getting hotter and hotter, so more people will eat ice cream, and tourists also like to eat ice cream,” Lee said. “They won’t wait for northbound consumption just to eat ice cream. A cup is only a few dozen dollars.”
Lee said foreign brands had been closely monitoring tourist arrival numbers, with the recent uptick encouraging them to expand their operations to Hong Kong.
The city welcomed 31.22 million visitors in the first seven months of 2026, an 11 per cent increase year on year.
The total value of Hong Kong’s retail sales rose for the 15th consecutive month in July, with the government reporting an uptick of 4.5 per cent from last year. Sales in the first seven months of the year grew by 8.9 per cent year on year.
Lee also noted that certain niche industries, such as traditional cafes, cigar stores and gold shops, were expanding alongside international brands to capitalise on cheaper leasing terms.

data.title: Machines now use AI more than humans, boosting cheap Chinese models
data.description:
The global artificial intelligence boom recently crossed a landmark threshold: autonomous agents now consume more than five times as much data as human users, triggering a surge in processing costs that is giving lower-priced Chinese models a competitive edge, according to analysts.
Unlike traditional chatbots that simply respond to human prompts, these agents operate independently to execute multi-step workflows, such as writing software, conducting research or managing business operations.
A single assignment can trigger a cascade of automated model calls as an agent plans its task, searches databases, invokes software tools and audits its own results.
This shift has dramatically altered the economics of AI deployment. Agentic requests consumed about 15 times more tokens – the basic units of data processed by an AI model – than standard human queries, according to data from model aggregator OpenRouter compiled by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
The data showed that daily token consumption from agentic workloads on OpenRouter hit 7.3 trillion in early August – 14 times the level six months earlier.
Agentic activity first surpassed human usage in February. By August, it accounted for over five times the 1.4 trillion tokens generated by human users on the platform.
Token usage will continue to grow exponentially as models become more capable and penetrate more scenarios
Sun Wenhao, TH Capital
Much of the increase came from cached prompt tokens – repeated portions of prompts, including system instructions, conversation histories and tool definitions, that can be reused without being fully processed again. Providers generally charge less for cached input because it requires less computation, although the rapid growth in overall volume could still increase corporate AI bills.
“Token usage will continue to grow exponentially as models become more capable and penetrate more scenarios,” said Sun Wenhao, a senior investment manager at Chinese deep tech venture investor TH Capital.
In China, daily token calls jumped 5,000-fold to 500 trillion in June this year from around 100 billion at the start of 2024, according to official data cited by state broadcaster CCTV.
To keep costs manageable, companies are increasingly turning to “model routing”, an approach where routine, repetitive tasks are directed to lower-cost models, reserving expensive, high-powered frontier models for complex reasoning, according to US enterprise software firm Salesforce.
“If everything runs on premium models, it is clearly too expensive,” Sun said, adding that coding and text-based research currently dominated agent usage, mostly assisting human workers rather than fully automating jobs.
Token demand could rise further once agents were trusted to carry out more tasks from beginning to end, he added.
The cost sensitivity could work to the advantage of Chinese open-weight models – AI systems that are released freely over the internet, allowing users with the necessary hardware to download and customise them for their own use.

For example, DeepSeek’s V4-Flash charges US$0.14 per million standard input tokens and US$0.28 per million output tokens. By comparison, OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol charges US$4 and US$20, respectively, while Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 costs US$10 and US$50.
DeepSeek accounted for 22.7 per cent of text requests on OpenRouter as of Thursday, the largest share of any model developer, ahead of Google’s 20.4 per cent and OpenAI’s 19.6 per cent, according to the platform’s live rankings.
However, cost is not the only hurdle facing widespread agent adoption.
Agents could generate code, analysis and documents faster than employees could vet them, potentially shifting the operational bottleneck from AI processing speed to human oversight, according to research from the MIT Sloan School of Management published in June.

data.title: Reduced visibility into the ‘thinking’ of OpenAI’s new model sparks safety fears
data.description:
OpenAI’s new model, GPT-6 Astra, has less direct visibility into how a model thinks, a development that has sparked concerns coming just weeks after the Hugging Face hacking incident that required a Chinese open model to investigate, according to analysts.
When announcing Astra on Thursday, OpenAI said it was “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model,” with a “significant jump in cyber capabilities”.
OpenAI president Greg Brockman said at the end of a press call announcing Astra’s arrival that it likely represents AGI, or artificial general intelligence – AI that matches or outperforms human intelligence.
However, OpenAI also said the model’s written reasoning was “harder to monitor” compared with GPT-5.6 Sol, the previous generation released in July.
“We have found that GPT-6 Astra is more capable of controlling its own CoT (chain of thought) than GPT-5.6 Sol, and less likely to include incriminating information in its CoT,” OpenAI said, referring to the intermediate reasoning steps an AI generates while solving a task.
The shift in visibility stems from a technique known as recurrent depth, or looped transformers, which reuses parts of a neural network. As a result, it processes complex logic inside hidden mathematical loops rather than in step-by-step readable text, The Information reported on Tuesday ahead of the launch.
OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki on X called the report “confusing”, without naming the media.
OpenAI did not disclose architectural details of the new system. A company representative said in a statement to the South China Morning Post on Friday that the decline in monitorability was “a real challenge that [it] takes seriously”.
The representative added that the new model does not use “neuralese”, a controversial technique where AI reasons internally using mathematical representations rather than words.
As frontier AI labs race to squeeze greater intelligence out of increasingly expensive computing infrastructure, the decrease in visibility has drawn global attention, especially after OpenAI’s agents breached the Hugging Face platform in July, highlighting the importance of being able to inspect what models are thinking.

Is recurrent depth a bad thing?
Unlike existing AI architectures that pass text through a fixed series of computational layers to determine the next word, recurrent depth loops the data through these layers repeatedly. This approach can have a positive impact on performance and costs.
Hamish Low, research associate at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, said it may “reduce the amount of memory required by having a smaller model repeat some of its internal processing” amid growing memory chip costs.
The technique effectively buys “greater reasoning depth with fewer weights and potentially lower memory requirements,” said Wei Sun, principal analyst for artificial intelligence at Counterpoint Research.
However, this approach reduces “the amount of reasoning humans can directly inspect,” which “creates an emerging intelligence-versus-observability trade-off”, Sun said.

What are the security concerns?
Reading the chain-of-thought reasoning can be critical for understanding the high-profile Hugging Face incident, analysts said.
“Having much of the reasoning occur in a closed box rather than by ‘thinking out loud’ through normal human language will make it much harder to understand how these AI systems are operating,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution.
Researchers investigating the Hugging Face incident were able to reconstruct the agents’ behaviour partly by examining their written chains of thought.
When Hugging Face detected the intrusion, its security team initially tried using commercial frontier AI models to help analyse the incoming attack, but those requests were blocked by the providers’ automated safety guardrails. Consequently, it opted to run Z.ai’s open-weight model, GLM-5.2, locally to contain the attack.
“The fact that the Hugging Face incident happened, and then right afterwards, they are releasing a model that’s harder to monitor – that’s why so many people are freaked out,” said Ben Hayum, research assistant for the Technology and National Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security (CNAS).
“If we keep getting substantial gains in the internal processing we can do without external visibility into it, AI model alignment becomes a lot harder from the get-go in terms of creating a safe model,” he added.
Are Chinese AI firms adopting it?
Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, has started looking into the looped transformer architectures. In an earnings call earlier this week, company founder Tang Jie discussed using a “Loop Transformer” to increase the effective depth of its models and described the direction of its next-generation GLM-6 model as “self-evolution”.
Analysts said this technique was attractive to Chinese developers, given their limited access to advanced compute resources.
Low at the AI policy institute said Chinese AI firms might have stronger incentives to adopt it amid ongoing price wars, but it depended on how large the benefits were. “The hardware they have, their research priorities and training data, and how they balance lower costs against speed and model performance also affect their decisions,” he added.
Counterpoint’s Sun said the technique could be attractive, but it “should be viewed as compute reallocation, not free compute.”
“The same economics apply in the US too,” she added.
It remained to be seen whether other companies follow suit, said Jinge Wang, an AI safety research engineer at Concordia AI.
If AI companies’ primary goal was to enhance capabilities, model interpretability and monitorability would “inevitably deteriorate”, Wang said.
Additional reporting by Vincent Chow

data.title: Hong Kong Disneyland Hotel to close from October 12 for major renovation
data.description:
Hong Kong Disneyland Hotel will temporarily close from October 12 for a comprehensive renovation and upgrade, with no completion date announced, as the resort shifts focus to seasonal culinary offerings and immersive storytelling.
Hong Kong Disneyland announced on Friday that the Victorian-style property, open since 2005, will be revamped with Disney movie-themed rooms, while retaining the hotel’s classic charm.
“As the world’s only Disney resort backed by mountains and facing the sea, this place perfectly blends Disney magic with natural scenery, bringing guests a unique holiday experience,” said Anita Lai Pui-shan, vice-president of communications and public affairs.
“The renovated hotel will retain its classic charm while integrating immersive story experiences, innovative design and better service, further consolidating Hong Kong Disneyland’s leading position in regional tourism.”
The closure leaves the resort’s two other properties to absorb demand. Disney Explorers Lodge offers 750 rooms while Disney’s Hollywood Hotel has 600 rooms.
Lai noted that average occupancy across all three hotels exceeded 80 per cent during the recent summer holiday, in line with the broader Hong Kong market.
Over the coming months, the resort will continue to roll out Halloween- and Christmas-themed dining, including some halal-certified offerings.
The seasonal line-up includes the return of “Jack Skellington’s The Nightmare Before Dinner”, featuring theatrical lighting and smoke effects, alongside Christmas Frozen-themed treats in the World of Frozen area.
Meanwhile, the hotel’s Crystal Lotus restaurant – famed for its 2,238 crystal lotus entrance and Disney character dim sum – will be unavailable until the renovation is completed.
